# A ball that contains two balls, one-limb center

Kernel `ball_hull_1` · **UNVERIFIED** · [all operations](index.md) · [how to read this page](reading.md)

## What it computes

A ball that contains the union of two balls, $X$ the ball of center $c_x$ and radius $r_x$ and $Y$ the ball of center $c_y$ and radius $r_y$; the empty set and the whole line included:

$$Z \supseteq X \cup Y.$$

## C++

**Not yet called by the public headers.** No public operation computes this kernel yet.

## Requires

- $X$, of center $c_x$ and radius $r_x$, is a canonical ball: a finite ball (finite center, finite radius $\ge 0$), the whole line (center 0, radius $+\infty$), or the empty set (every limb a NaN).
- $Y$, of center $c_y$ and radius $r_y$, is a canonical ball: a finite ball (finite center, finite radius $\ge 0$), the whole line (center 0, radius $+\infty$), or the empty set (every limb a NaN).

## Target (not proved)

For operands that satisfy the requirements, finite, infinite or NaN:

- The result, the ball $Z$ of center $c_z$ and radius $r_z$, is a canonical ball.
- $Z$ contains every member of $X$ and every member of $Y$.
- $Z$ is empty exactly when $X$ and $Y$ both are; when one is empty, $Z$ is the other, as it is (the same limbs).
- Not claimed: that $Z$ is the smallest such ball.

Stated for every binary format with a precision of at least 2 bits, rounding to nearest with ties to even and with gradual underflow, in the IEEE model, with signed zeros, infinities, NaN and overflow. Both limb types qualify: `double` has 53 bits, `float` has 24 bits.

## Source

**Algorithm:** both balls to intervals, their hull, back to a ball (Milestone 2 listing). **License:** algorithm and proof: MIT.

## Listing

From [`gen/kernels/ball_hull_1.kernel`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/gen/kernels/ball_hull_1.kernel), the description the C++ and the formal model (`proofs/gen/IeeeModel.v`) are generated from. Each line is one operation of `T`; one that rounds rounds to nearest, and `prod(a, b)` is $\mathrm{RN}(ab)$, written as a fused multiply-add with a zero addend ([the kernel IR](../developer/architecture.md#the-kernel-ir)).
It calls [`ball_to_interval_1`](ball_to_interval_1.md), [`interval_hull_1`](interval_hull_1.md), [`interval_to_ball_1`](interval_to_ball_1.md).

```
# A ball with a one-limb center that contains two such balls (milestone2.md, "One enclosure
# interface", "Hull, intersection and split of balls"): both balls to intervals (ball_to_interval_1,
# the smallest intervals of T that contain them), the hull of the intervals (interval_hull_1), back to
# a ball (interval_to_ball_1). If X is empty Y is returned as it is, and if Y is empty and X is not, X
# (the same limbs), by the tests of the radii (a NaN radius is the empty ball); the composition alone
# would return it converted twice. Two empty balls give Y, whose NaNs need not be X's, which is why
# the second clause has its condition. The whole line gives the whole line through the conversions.
# The selects choose the composition when both operands are not empty (qx, qy), the case the scalar
# printer puts first. Not claimed: the smallest such ball.

(xl, xu) = ball_to_interval_1(cx, rx)
(yl, yu) = ball_to_interval_1(cy, ry)
(zl, zu) = interval_hull_1(xl, xu, yl, yu)
(c, r)   = interval_to_ball_1(zl, zu)
qx       = eq(rx, rx)
qy       = eq(ry, ry)
ca       = select(qy, c, cx)
ra       = select(qy, r, rx)
cz       = select(qx, ca, cy)
rz       = select(qx, ra, ry)
```
